all\_prime\_bases\_right\_half\_positive=true\\
prime\_base\_count=669\\
minimum\_left\_oppermann\_count=1\\
finite\_evidence\_not\_used\_as\_global\_proof=true.
\end{quote}
This finite audit is only structural evidence.  The theorem identifies the
true top-row subcore; it does not prove Oppermann's half-window or the
row/column theorem unconditionally.
\end{proof}


\begin{theorem}[Finite sqrt-gap bridge and square-phase tail]
Let \(P\) be prime and \(1<k<P\), and put \(x=kP\).  Since
\(\sqrt{x}<P\), any theorem guaranteeing a prime in
\([x,x+\sqrt{x}]\) gives
\[
  N_P(k)=\pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)\ge1.
\]
Using the finite sqrt-gap input
\[
  117\le x\le 10^{18}
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  [x,x+\sqrt{x}]\hbox{ contains a prime},
\]
the strict rows with \(kP\le10^{18}\) are therefore closed, after a direct
finite check of the rows with \(kP<117\).  For the top row
\(x=P^2-P\), this finite bridge reaches every prime base
\[
  P\le 999999937.
\]
Beyond this range the same top-row failure is exactly the square-phase low
sieve full cover
\[
  N_{\rm top}(P)=0
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \forall\,1\le r<P,\quad
  \gcd\!\left(P^2-r,\prod_{q<P}q\right)>1,
\]
equivalently the interval \(1\le r<P\) is covered by the residue classes
\[
  r\equiv P^2\pmod q,\qquad q<P,\ q\ {\rm prime}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The bridge inequality \(\sqrt{kP}<P\) is immediate from \(k<P\).  Hence a
prime in \([x,x+\sqrt{x}]\) lies before \((k+1)P\); because the endpoints are
composite in the strict range, this is exactly positivity of the Phi--LPF
endpoint difference.  The finite sqrt-gap input is Lemma 2.7 of
Erdos--Harcos--Kharel--Maga--Mezei--Toroczkai, based on the computed prime-gap
tables of Oliveira e Silva--Herzog--Pardi.  The direct subthreshold audit
checks \(49\) strict rows and finds minimum prime count \(1\).  Solving
\(P^2-P\le10^{18}\) gives integer bound \(P\le10^9\), and the largest prime
base not exceeding that bound is \(999999937\).

The last equivalence is the same least-prime-factor ownership identity applied
to the top row \(P^2-P<n<P^2\).  If no top-row entry is prime, then each
\(P^2-r\) has a least prime factor \(q<P\), because \(P^2-r<P^2\).  Conversely,
if every \(P^2-r\) is divisible by some \(q<P\), no top-row entry is prime.
For each fixed \(q\), this divisibility is exactly
\(r\equiv P^2\pmod q\).  Thus the remaining infinite tail is not a finite
verification problem; it is the named square-phase special long-cover problem.

The certificate is recorded in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

sqrt-square-phase-tail-router.md.
\end{quote}
It records

small\_checked\_row\_count=49\\
all\_small\_rows\_positive=true\\
largest\_prime\_base\_with\_top\_row\_start\_le\_x\_max=999999937.
\end{quote}
This theorem closes only the declared finite segment.  The row/column theorem
still requires
\(\texttt{SquarePhaseTailLongBlockPDECExclusion}\), a uniform rough-survivor
lower bound, or a genuine global square-root-scale short-interval theorem.
\end{proof}


\begin{theorem}[Top-row half-rough semiprime shadow]
For a prime \(P\), define
\[
  R_{1/2}(P)
  =
  \#\left\{1\le r<P:
  \gcd\!\left(P^2-r,\prod_{q\le P/2}q\right)=1\right\},
\]
where \(q\) runs over primes, and define the reciprocal semiprime shadow
\[
  T_{1/2}(P)
  =
  \sum_{\substack{P/2<q<P\\ q\ {\rm prime}}}
  \#\left\{m\ {\rm prime}:
  \left\lfloor \frac{P^2-P}{q}\right\rfloor
  <m\le
  \left\lfloor \frac{P^2-1}{q}\right\rfloor
  \right\}.
\]
Then
\[
  \pi(P^2-1)-\pi(P^2-P)=R_{1/2}(P)-T_{1/2}(P).
\]
Consequently the prime-indexed Oppermann-left top row is positive exactly when
the half-rough survivor count strictly exceeds this reciprocal semiprime
shadow.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The half-rough survivor set consists of the top-row entries \(P^2-r\) not
divisible by any prime \(q\le P/2\).  Such a survivor is either prime or
composite.  If it is composite, its least prime factor \(q\) must satisfy
\(P/2<q<P\), since \(P^2-r<P^2\).  Write \(P^2-r=qm\).  The top-row
inequality \(P^2-P<P^2-r<P^2\) gives
\[
  \frac{P^2-P}{q}<m<\frac{P^2}{q},
\]
and because \(q<P\) and \(q>P/2\), this puts \(m\) in \((P,2P)\).  For
\(P\ge11\), \(m\) cannot be composite: all prime factors of \(m\) would be at
least \(q>P/2\), forcing \(m\ge q^2>2P\).  The small prime bases are checked
directly in the finite audit.  Thus every composite half-rough survivor is
counted exactly once by the displayed \(T_{1/2}\), and every term of
\(T_{1/2}\) gives a composite top-row survivor.  Subtracting the shadow from
the half-rough survivor set leaves precisely the prime top-row entries.

For each fixed \(q\in(P/2,P)\), the admissible \(m\)-window has length \(P/q<2\),
so the shadow is a sparse reciprocal prime-pair graph, not a full LPF tree.
The certificate is recorded in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
docs/monograph/prime-matrix-phi-lpf-top-row-half-\\
rough-semiprime-shadow-router.md.
\end{quote}
It records
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

all\_half\_rough\_identities\_hold=true\\
minimum\_half\_rough\_minus\_shadow=1\\
P=5003:\ R\_1/2=330,\ T\_1/2=49,\ direct\_top\_primes=281.
\end{quote}
This theorem is an exact reduction.  It does not prove the uniform inequality
\(R_{1/2}(P)>T_{1/2}(P)\) in the infinite tail, but it makes the next hard point
the named
\(\texttt{HalfRoughSurvivorExcessOverReciprocalSemiprimeShadow}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict-\(k\) external bulk and square-band partition]
For \(x=kP\) with \(1<k<P\), the Phi--LPF endpoint difference gives the exact
count
\[
  N_P(k)=\pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP).
\]
The finite square-root input closes the initial segment \(kP\le 10^{18}\).
Dusart's explicit interval closes only the logarithmic subband
\[
  k\le 25\log^2(kP),
\]
and the Baker--Harman--Pintz \(x^{21/40}\) input, when its asymptotic threshold
is available, closes the bulk subband
\[
  P\ge (kP)^{21/40}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad k\le P^{19/21}.
\]
Therefore any strict-\(k\) counterexample not already handled by these external
arms must lie in the high square-edge band
\[
  kP>10^{18},\qquad P^{19/21}<k<P.
\]
The top row \(k=P-1\) has the sharper half-rough semiprime-shadow interface
\(R_{1/2}(P)>T_{1/2}(P)\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The certificate is recorded in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
docs/monograph/prime-matrix-phi-lpf-strict-k-external-bulk-\\
square-band-partition-router.md.
\end{quote}
It records

finite\_sqrt\_initial\_segment=kP<=10\string^18\\
remaining\_high\_k\_band=P\string^(19/21)<k<P.
\end{quote}
This is a partition theorem, not a closure theorem.  It shows that the present
external-route residue is no longer all strict rows, but the named high-\(k\)
square band; closing that band still requires a genuine square-root-scale short
interval theorem, a structural Phi--LPF excess, or a semiprime-shadow/PDEC
exclusion.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Strict-\(k\) half-rough shadow band split]
Let \(P\) be prime and \(1<k<P\).  Define
\[
  R_{1/2}(P,k)
  =
  \#\left\{1\le t<P:
  \gcd\!\left(kP+t,\prod_{q\le P/2}q\right)=1\right\},
\]
where \(q\) runs over primes, and
\[
  T_{1/2}(P,k)
  =
  \#\left\{(q,m):
  q,m\ {\rm prime},\ P/2<q\le m<2P,\ kP<qm<(k+1)P\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)=R_{1/2}(P,k)-T_{1/2}(P,k).
\]
Moreover, if \(4((k+1)P-1)\le P^2\), then \(T_{1/2}(P,k)=0\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
Any composite survivor counted by \(R_{1/2}(P,k)\) has least prime factor
\(q>P/2\).  Since the number is below \(P^2\), this \(q\) is also below \(P\).
Writing \(kP+t=qm\), one has \(m<2P\).  For \(P\ge 11\), \(m\) cannot be
composite, because all its prime factors would be at least \(q>P/2\), forcing
\(m\ge q^2>P^2/4>2P\).  Taking \(q\le m\) gives a unique two-prime shadow
representative for every composite half-rough survivor, and every such shadow
is composite and survives the \(q\le P/2\) deletion.  Subtraction leaves exactly
the primes in the row.  If \(4((k+1)P-1)\le P^2\), the whole row lies at or below
\(P^2/4\), while every product of two primes \(>P/2\) is strictly larger than
\(P^2/4\), so the shadow is empty.

The certificate is recorded in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

shadow-band-split-router.md.
\end{quote}
It records

identity\_failure\_count=0\\
next=HalfRoughSurvivorExistenceInShadowFreeHighBand\\
\phantom{next=}OR HighKHalfRoughSurvivorExcessOverTwoPrimeShadow.
\end{quote}
This is still a reduction, not a proof of the final positive core.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Shadow-free half-primorial special phase]
Let
\[
  M_{1/2}(P)=\prod_{\substack{q\le P/2\\ q\ {\rm prime}}}q .
\]
In the shadow-free subband \(4((k+1)P-1)\le P^2\), the strict row is positive
if and only if
\[
  \exists\,1\le t<P\quad \gcd(kP+t,M_{1/2}(P))=1.
\]
Equivalently, a failure in this subband is exactly the assertion that the
special phase \(kP+1\bmod M_{1/2}(P)\) starts a covered block of length \(P-1\)
in the half-primorial period.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The previous theorem gives \(T_{1/2}(P,k)=0\) in the stated subband.  Thus a
row prime is the same object as a half-rough survivor after deleting all primes
\(q\le P/2\), which is precisely a residue coprime to \(M_{1/2}(P)\).  Since the
whole row lies below \(P^2/4\), any such survivor is automatically prime: a
composite with no prime factor \(\le P/2\) would be a product of at least two
factors \(>P/2\), hence would exceed \(P^2/4\).  The residue formulation follows
by reducing the interval \(kP+1,\ldots,kP+P-1\) modulo \(M_{1/2}(P)\).

The certificate is recorded in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

primorial-phase-router.md.
\end{quote}
It records

next=HalfPrimorialSpecialPhaseAvoidsLongCoveredBlockOrPDEC.
\end{quote}
The finite scans are evidence only.  Global closure still needs either a
half-primorial Jacobsthal bound at this scale, or a special-phase avoidance/PDEC
argument.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Upper-band reciprocal two-prime shadow]
Let \(P\) be prime and \(1<k<P\).  In the upper square band
\[
  4((k+1)P-1)>P^2,
\]
the two-prime shadow from the strict-\(k\) half-rough split has the exact
reciprocal-window form
\[
  T_{1/2}(P,k)
  =
  \sum_{\substack{P/2<q<P\\ q\ {\rm prime}}}
  \#\{m\in I_q(P,k):m\ {\rm prime}\},
\]
where
\[
  I_q(P,k)
  =
  \left[
    \max\!\left(q,\left\lfloor\frac{kP}{q}\right\rfloor+1\right),
    \left\lfloor\frac{(k+1)P-1}{q}\right\rfloor
  \right]\cap{\mathbb Z}.
\]
Moreover \(|I_q(P,k)|\le2\) for every such \(q\).  Hence an upper-band row
failure is exactly a sparse reciprocal prime-pair saturation of the half-rough
survivors, or a named half-rough-floor / reciprocal-shadow-ceiling defect.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The previous half-rough split counts composite survivors by products
\(qm\) with \(P/2<q\le m<2P\) and
\[
  kP<qm<(k+1)P .
\]
For a fixed \(q\), this inequality is equivalent to
\[
  \left\lfloor\frac{kP}{q}\right\rfloor+1
  \le m\le
  \left\lfloor\frac{(k+1)P-1}{q}\right\rfloor .
\]
The unique representative convention \(q\le m\) supplies the additional lower
cutoff \(m\ge q\), giving the displayed \(I_q(P,k)\).  Its real length is
strictly less than \(P/q<2\), so it contains at most two integers.  Filtering
those at-most-two candidates by primality gives the actual two-prime shadow.

prime-shadow-excess-router.md.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

AND UpperBandHalfRoughFloorOrReciprocalPrimePairCeiling.
\end{quote}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Upper-band reciprocal shadow graph forest]
In the setting of the preceding theorem, form the bipartite graph whose left
vertices are primes \(q\in(P/2,P)\), whose right vertices are prime candidates
\(m\in[q,2P)\), and whose edges are the pairs \((q,m)\) with
\[
  kP<qm<(k+1)P .
\]
This reciprocal shadow graph has degree at most two on each side and is
ordered non-crossing.  In particular it is a forest.  Therefore an upper-band
counterexample cannot be produced by a cyclic shadow feedback; it must be a
forest-shadow saturation of all half-rough survivors, or a named PDEC.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The degree bound is the reciprocal-window bound in both directions.  For fixed
\(q\), the admissible \(m\)-interval has length \(<P/q<2\).  For fixed \(m\),
the admissible \(q\)-interval has length \(<P/m\le P/q<2\) because \(m\ge q\).
Thus both sides have degree at most two.

If two edges crossed in the ordered sense, say \(q_1<q_2\) but \(m_1<m_2\),
then
\[
  q_2m_2-q_1m_1
  =
  (q_2-q_1)m_2+q_1(m_2-m_1)>P,
\]
since all involved primes exceed \(P/2\) and distinct odd primes differ by at
least \(2\).  Two such products cannot both lie in the same interval of length
\(P\).  Hence the graph is non-crossing.  If a cycle existed, take the smallest
\(q_0\) on the cycle and let its two cycle-neighbours be \(m_a<m_b\).  Any edge
from another \(q>q_0\) to a vertex \(m>m_a\) would cross the edge
\((q_0,m_a)\), so \(m_b\) cannot have the second incident edge required by the
cycle.  This contradiction proves that the graph is a forest.

reciprocal-graph-structure-router.md.
\end{quote}

max\_prime=1009\\

\end{quote}
This still does not prove row positivity.  The remaining upper-band interface is
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

\end{quote}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Punctured half-primorial forest phase]
Let
\[
  M_{1/2}(P)=\prod_{\substack{q\le P/2\\q\ {\rm prime}}}q
\]
and let \(F(P,k)\) be the forest-hole set
\[
  F(P,k)=
  \{\,t: t=qm-kP,\ q,m\ {\rm prime},\ P/2<q\le m<2P,\ kP<qm<(k+1)P\,\}.
\]
Then the prime slots in the row \(kP+1,\ldots,kP+P-1\) are exactly
\[
  \{\,1\le t<P:\gcd(kP+t,M_{1/2}(P))=1,\ t\notin F(P,k)\,\}.
\]
Consequently the shadow-free lane is the zero-hole case \(F(P,k)=\varnothing\),
and an upper-band row failure is exactly a punctured half-primorial covered
block:
\[
  \{\,1\le t<P:\gcd(kP+t,M_{1/2}(P))=1\,\}\subseteq F(P,k).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
If \(t\) is coprime to \(M_{1/2}(P)\), then \(kP+t\) is not divisible by any
prime \(q\le P/2\).  If this number is composite, its least prime factor
satisfies \(P/2<q<P\).  Writing \(kP+t=qm\), one has \(m<2P\), and for
\(P\ge11\) the same least-prime-factor argument used above forces \(m\) to be
prime.  With the convention \(q\le m\), this composite survivor is counted
by exactly one element of \(F(P,k)\).  Conversely every element of \(F(P,k)\)
is a composite half-rough survivor.  Removing \(F(P,k)\) from the
half-primorial survivors leaves precisely the prime row slots.

\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

\end{quote}
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Punctured Phi--LPF endpoint difference]
Let \(p_{1/2}(P)\) be the least prime \(>P/2\), and define
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)
  =
  \Phi((k+1)P-1,p_{1/2}(P))-\Phi(kP,p_{1/2}(P)).
\]
Then for every prime \(P\) and \(1<k<P\),
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)
  =
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)-|F(P,k)|,
\]
where \(F(P,k)\) is the reciprocal forest-hole set of the previous theorem.
Thus the remaining strict-\(k\) counterexample condition is the endpoint
inequality
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)\le |F(P,k)|.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
By definition, \(\Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)\) counts exactly the entries in the row
whose least prime factor is at least \(p_{1/2}(P)\), equivalently those not
divisible by any prime \(q\le P/2\).  The preceding theorem says that the
composite entries among these are exactly the forest holes \(F(P,k)\).
Subtracting those holes leaves precisely the primes in the row.  The
shadow-free case is the subcase \(|F(P,k)|=0\); the upper-band case is the same
identity with a nonempty reciprocal forest.

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Punctured endpoint parity-capacity bound]
For a prime \(P\), \(1<k<P\), and a high prime \(q\in(P/2,P)\), put
\[
  I_q(P,k)=
  \left[
    \max\left(q,\left\lfloor \frac{kP}{q}\right\rfloor+1\right),
    \left\lfloor \frac{(k+1)P-1}{q}\right\rfloor
  \right]\cap{\bf Z}.
\]
Let
\[
  W_{\rm int}(P,k)=\sum_{P/2<q<P}|I_q(P,k)|
\]
and let \(E_{\rm even}(P,k)\) be the number of pairs \((q,m)\), with
\(q\) prime in \((P/2,P)\) and \(m\in I_q(P,k)\), for which \(m>2\) is even.
Set
\[
  C_{\rm par}(P,k)=W_{\rm int}(P,k)-E_{\rm even}(P,k).
\]
Then
\[
  |F(P,k)|\le C_{\rm par}(P,k).
\]
Consequently
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)>C_{\rm par}(P,k)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)>0.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The reciprocal-window theorem shows that every forest hole is represented by
a pair \((q,m)\) with \(q\) prime in \((P/2,P)\), \(m\in I_q(P,k)\), and
\(m\) prime.  The first bound \(|F(P,k)|\le W_{\rm int}(P,k)\) is therefore
pure containment.  If \(m>2\) is even, it cannot be prime, hence each such
candidate may be deleted from the prime-candidate ceiling.  This gives
\(|F(P,k)|\le C_{\rm par}(P,k)\).  Combining with the preceding exact endpoint
identity gives the displayed positivity implication.

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Punctured endpoint \(6\)-wheel capacity bound]
For a prime \(P\), \(1<k<P\), and the reciprocal windows \(I_q(P,k)\) above,
let \(E_{2,3}(P,k)\) be the number of pairs \((q,m)\) with
\[
  P/2<q<P,\qquad q\ {\rm prime},\qquad m\in I_q(P,k),
\]
such that \(m\) is forced composite by the \(6\)-wheel, namely
\[
  (m>2,\ 2\mid m)\quad\hbox{or}\quad (m>3,\ 3\mid m).
\]
Set
\[
  C_6(P,k)=W_{\rm int}(P,k)-E_{2,3}(P,k).
\]
Then
\[
  |F(P,k)|\le C_6(P,k).
\]
Consequently
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)>C_6(P,k)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)>0.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The proof is the same reciprocal-window containment as in the parity-capacity
bound, with one additional Euler \(6\)-wheel deletion.  If \(m>2\) is even, or
if \(m>3\) is divisible by \(3\), then \(m\) is not prime and cannot be the
cofactor of a prime-pair forest hole.  Deleting all such candidates from the
integer windows gives \(|F(P,k)|\le C_6(P,k)\).  The endpoint positivity
implication follows from
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)=\Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)-|F(P,k)|.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Punctured endpoint \(30\)-wheel capacity bound]
For a prime \(P\), \(1<k<P\), and the reciprocal windows \(I_q(P,k)\) above,
let \(E_{2,3,5}(P,k)\) be the number of pairs \((q,m)\) with
\[
  P/2<q<P,\qquad q\ {\rm prime},\qquad m\in I_q(P,k),
\]
such that \(m\) is forced composite by the \(30\)-wheel, namely
\[
  (m>2,\ 2\mid m),\qquad (m>3,\ 3\mid m),\qquad
  (m>5,\ 5\mid m).
\]
Set
\[
  C_{30}(P,k)=W_{\rm int}(P,k)-E_{2,3,5}(P,k).
\]
Then
\[
  |F(P,k)|\le C_{30}(P,k).
\]
Consequently
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)>C_{30}(P,k)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)>0.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
This is the same reciprocal-window containment as in the \(6\)-wheel bound,
with the next Euler-wheel deletion included.  A forest hole requires the
cofactor \(m\) to be prime.  Hence every candidate \(m>5\) divisible by \(5\)
is impossible, just as the preceding layer deleted even \(m>2\) and
\(3\)-divisible \(m>3\).  Deleting all candidates forced composite by
\(2,3,\) or \(5\) gives \(|F(P,k)|\le C_{30}(P,k)\).  The endpoint positivity
implication again follows from
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)=\Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)-|F(P,k)|.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Primorial-wheel limit is exact but not an independent proof]
The \(30\)-wheel capacity bound extends monotonically to every primorial
wheel.  If \(S\) is a finite set of primes and \(C_S(P,k)\) denotes the
reciprocal-window capacity after deleting all \(m\in I_q(P,k)\) with
\[
  m>\ell,\qquad \ell\mid m,\qquad \ell\in S,
\]
then \(S_1\subseteq S_2\) implies
\[
  C_{S_2}(P,k)\le C_{S_1}(P,k).
\]
In particular the chain
\[
  2,\quad 2\cdot3,\quad 2\cdot3\cdot5,\quad
  2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7,\quad\ldots
\]
gives a genuine sequence of sharper forest-hole ceilings.

However, once \(S\) contains all primes \(\ell\le\sqrt{2P-1}\), the capacity
is exact:
\[
  C_S(P,k)=|F(P,k)|.
\]
Consequently
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)-C_S(P,k)
  =\pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP).
\]
Thus the primorial-wheel limit is an exact restatement of the target row
positivity, not an independent proof of it.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
Monotonicity is immediate: enlarging \(S\) only deletes more cofactor
candidates that are forced composite.  For exactness, every reciprocal
cofactor satisfies \(m<2P\).  If such an \(m\) is composite, it has a prime
factor \(\ell\le\sqrt{m}\le\sqrt{2P-1}\).  Hence the dynamic wheel containing
all primes up to \(\sqrt{2P-1}\) deletes every composite \(m\), while a prime
\(m\) is not deleted by the rule \(m>\ell,\ \ell\mid m\).  The survivors are
therefore exactly the prime cofactors, counted with the same \(q\)-window
multiplicity as \(F(P,k)\).

Combining this with the endpoint identity
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)=\Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)-|F(P,k)|
\]
gives the displayed equality.  The machine certificate is archived in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
docs/monograph/prime-matrix-phi-lpf-primorial-wheel-limit-audit.md.
\end{quote}
It records, for \(P\le1009\),
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

all\_exact\_capacity\_equals\_holes=true\\
all\_exact\_margin\_equals\_direct\_prime\_count=true.
\end{quote}
For example, at \(P=1009,k=1008\),
\[
  W_{\rm int}=101,\qquad C_{30}=28,\qquad
  C_{210}=27,\qquad C_{2310}=26,\qquad C_{\sqrt{2P}}=19=|F|.
\]
This narrows the bookkeeping interface to
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
PuncturedSqrtWheelExactForestHolePositivityOr\\
SignedDispersionOrSpecialSquarePhaseLowerBound.
\end{quote}
No unconditional row/column closure follows from the wheel limit alone.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Fixed-wheel rough-composite residual decomposition]
Let \(S\) be a finite set of wheel primes and let \(C_S(P,k)\) be the
reciprocal-window capacity obtained by deleting every candidate \(m\in
I_q(P,k)\) for which
\[
  m>\ell,\qquad \ell\mid m,\qquad \ell\in S .
\]
Define the fixed-wheel rough-composite residual
\[
  R_S(P,k)=\#\{(q,m): P/2<q<P,\ q\ {\rm prime},\ m\in I_q(P,k),\
  m\ {\rm composite},\ m\ {\rm is\ not\ deleted\ by}\ S\}.
\]
Then
\[
  C_S(P,k)=|F(P,k)|+R_S(P,k),
\]
and therefore
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)-C_S(P,k)
  =
  \bigl(\pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)\bigr)-R_S(P,k).
\]
Consequently a fixed-wheel positivity proof
\[
  \Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)>C_S(P,k)
\]
is exactly the stronger dominance assertion
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)>R_S(P,k).
\]
If \(S\) contains all primes \(\ell\le\sqrt{2P-1}\), then \(R_S(P,k)=0\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The candidates counted by \(C_S(P,k)\) are precisely the reciprocal-window
pairs \((q,m)\) that survive the \(S\)-wheel forced-composite deletion.  Each
surviving \(m\) is either prime or composite.  The prime alternatives are
exactly the forest holes \(F(P,k)\), counted with the same \(q\)-window
multiplicity; the composite alternatives are, by definition, \(R_S(P,k)\).
This proves \(C_S=|F|+R_S\).

Subtracting this identity from the endpoint formula
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)=\Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)-|F(P,k)|
\]
gives the displayed residual equation.  If \(S\) contains all primes up to
\(\sqrt{2P-1}\), then every composite \(m<2P\) has a prime factor in \(S\)
and is deleted; hence \(R_S=0\).

\]

\end{quote}

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[LPF shell decrement law for fixed-wheel residuals]
For each composite reciprocal cofactor \(m\), let \(r={\rm LPF}(m)\).  Then
\[
  m=r a,\qquad a\ge r,
\]
and \(a\) has no prime factor below \(r\).  Let
\[
  {\rm Shell}_r(P,k)
\]
denote the number of reciprocal-window pairs \((q,m)\) with
\({\rm LPF}(m)=r\), counted with the same multiplicity as in the forest-hole
ledger.  If \(C_y(P,k)\) denotes the primorial-wheel capacity after deleting
all cofactor candidates with least prime factor at most \(y\), then
\[
  R_y(P,k)=\sum_{r>y}{\rm Shell}_r(P,k),
\]
and for two cutoffs \(y<y'\),
\[
  C_y(P,k)-C_{y'}(P,k)
  =
  \sum_{y<r\le y'}{\rm Shell}_r(P,k).
\]
Thus each primorial-wheel promotion strips exactly the next LPF shell, and the
remaining fixed-wheel hard point is the tail dominance
\[
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)
  >
  \sum_{r>y}{\rm Shell}_r(P,k).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The factorization assertion is the defining property of the least prime
factor: if \(r={\rm LPF}(m)\), then \(m=ra\), \(a\ge r\), and no prime below
\(r\) divides \(a\).  Hence the composite cofactor candidates are partitioned
disjointly by their least prime factor.  A primorial wheel with cutoff \(y\)
deletes exactly those composite candidates whose least prime factor is at most
\(y\), while it leaves the prime cofactors untouched.  Therefore the residual
after the cutoff is precisely the shell tail \(\sum_{r>y}{\rm Shell}_r\), and
the drop from cutoff \(y\) to cutoff \(y'\) is the intervening shell sum.

diagnostics, but they do not by themselves prove this reciprocal-window
weighted, pointwise, same-row dominance statement.  No unconditional
row/column closure follows from the shell ledger alone.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Adjacent-coprime parity trap after the \(30\)-wheel]
Let \(n=qm\) be a \(30\)-wheel rough-composite residual candidate in the
reciprocal-window ledger.  Put \(r={\rm LPF}(m)\) and \(m=ra\).  Then
\[
  q,\ m,\ r,\ a
\]
are all odd, and \(r\ge7\).  Hence the adjacent-coprime identities
\[
  (qm,qm\pm1)=1,\qquad (m,m\pm1)=1,\qquad (a,a\pm1)=1
\]
do not create a prime channel: every integer \(qm\pm1\), \(m\pm1\), and
\(a\pm1\) occurring here is even and larger than \(2\), hence composite.
Moreover the quotient-adjacent lift
\[
  q r(a\pm1)=qra\pm qr
\]
cannot stay in the same row, because \(q>P/2\) and \(r\ge7\), so \(qr>P\).
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The \(30\)-wheel residual has already removed all cofactor candidates divisible
by \(2,3,\) or \(5\).  Thus a composite residual cofactor \(m\) has
\({\rm LPF}(m)=r\ge7\), and \(m,r\) are odd.  Since \(a=m/r\), the quotient
\(a\) is odd.  Also \(q\in(P/2,P)\) is an odd prime in the strict rows under
discussion.  Therefore \(qm\), \(m\), and \(a\) are odd.  Their adjacent
integers are even.  The lower adjacent values are also larger than \(2\):
\(m-1\ge6\), \(a-1\ge6\), and \(qm-1>2\).  Hence all these adjacent integers
are composite despite being coprime to their source.

For the quotient lift, changing \(a\) to \(a\pm1\) changes \(qra\) by
\(\pm qr\).  Since \(q>P/2\) and \(r\ge7\), this displacement is larger than
the row length \(P\).  Thus the quotient-adjacent object cannot be a same-row
prime payment.

one supplies a matching Type-I/Type-II or bilinear theorem for the present

OR same-object Type-II signed dispersion\\
OR square-phase endpoint lower bound.
\end{quote}
No unconditional row/column closure follows from adjacent coprimality alone.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[LPF tail reciprocal-graph Type--II obligation]
The \(30\)-wheel LPF tail residual has the exact representation
\[
  \begin{aligned}
  R_{30}(P,k)=
  \#\{(q,r,a):\ &P/2<q<P,\ q\ {\rm prime},\
  m=ra\in I_q(P,k),\\
  &r={\rm LPF}(m)\ge 7,\ a\ge r,\ a\ {\rm is}\ r{\rm -rough}\},
  \end{aligned}
\]
where
\[
  I_q(P,k)=
  \bigl[\max(q,\lfloor kP/q\rfloor+1),\
        \min(2P-1,\lfloor((k+1)P-1)/q\rfloor)\bigr].
\]
This representation is a balanced \(q\)-\(m\) object in scale, but its support
is not a rectangular Type--II box.  It is a same-row reciprocal graph with
thin fibres:
\[
  \#I_q(P,k)\le 2,\qquad
  \#\{q:m\in I_q(P,k)\}\le 2,\qquad
  \#\{a:kP<qra<(k+1)P\}\le 1 .
\]
Consequently a Ford--Maynard or Heath-Brown style Type--II continuation must
prove dispersion for this exact reciprocal graph.  It cannot be replaced by
adjacent coprimality, ordinary rough-number density, or a rectangular bilinear
box estimate.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The preceding LPF shell ledger partitions each \(30\)-wheel residual cofactor
\(m\) by \(r={\rm LPF}(m)\).  Since the \(30\)-wheel has removed factors
\(2,3,5\), every residual composite has \(r\ge7\) and \(m=ra\) with \(a\ge r\)
and \(a\) \(r\)-rough.  This gives the displayed triple representation.

The fibre bounds are deterministic.  For fixed \(q>P/2\), the row condition
\(kP<qm<(k+1)P\) gives an \(m\)-interval of length \(P/q<2\), hence at most
two integers after intersecting with the reciprocal cofactor range.  Conversely,
for fixed \(m\ge q>P/2\), the admissible \(q\)-interval has length \(P/m<2\).
Finally, for fixed \(q\) and \(r\), the admissible \(a\)-interval has length
\[
  \frac{P}{qr}<1,
\]
because \(q>P/2\) and \(r\ge7\).  Thus each \((q,r)\)-fibre contains at most
one \(a\).  In particular there is no quotient-fibre cancellation to harvest
inside a single \((q,r)\) line; any Type--II cancellation must run across the
moving reciprocal graph itself.

\begin{theorem}[CRT signed residue projection gate for the LPF tail]
Fix a wheel \(S\), put \(W_S=\prod_{\ell\in S}\ell\), and let \(R_S(P,k)\)
be the corresponding rough-composite residual.  For each residue class
\(a\bmod W_S\), define the same-row signed residue measure
\[
  \mu_S(a;P,k)
  =
  \#\{n:kP<n<(k+1)P,\ n\ {\rm prime},\ n\equiv a\pmod {W_S}\}
\]
\[
  \qquad
  -\#\{n=qm:kP<n<(k+1)P,\ n\equiv a\pmod {W_S},\
        (q,m)\ {\rm counted\ by}\ R_S(P,k)\}.
\]
Then
\[
  \sum_{a\bmod W_S}\mu_S(a;P,k)
  =
  \pi((k+1)P-1)-\pi(kP)-R_S(P,k).
\]
If \(P>2\max S\), all atoms in this signed measure lie in unit classes
modulo \(W_S\).

However, fixed CRT classwise dominance
\[
  \mu_S(a;P,k)\ge0\qquad\hbox{for every unit }a\bmod W_S
\]
is false as a route to the LPF-tail inequality.  The remaining CRT route must
therefore be a character-averaged or cross-residue signed dispersion theorem,
not a unit-cell matching argument.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The identity is just the partition of the signed row measure by residue class
modulo \(W_S\).  If \(P>2\max S\), then every high prime \(q\in(P/2,P)\) is
outside \(S\).  A row prime \(n>2\max S\) is also not divisible by any
\(\ell\in S\).  The \(S\)-wheel residual has cofactor \(m\) not deleted by
any \(\ell\in S\).  Hence both the prime atoms and the residual atoms are
unit classes modulo \(W_S\).

The classwise nonnegativity assertion is not a theorem.  The machine
certificate is archived in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

residue-projection-gate-audit.md.

\begin{proposition}[Phi--LPF exactness does not bypass the parity barrier]
The Phi--LPF identities above are combinatorially exact identities for
\(N_P(k)\).  They do not, by themselves, constitute a positive lower bound for
\(N_P(k)\).  In the top strict band \(k\asymp P\), the row starts at
\(x=kP\asymp P^2\) and has length \(P\asymp\sqrt{x}\).  Therefore any closure
that proceeds only by an ordinary short-interval theorem
\([x,x+x^\theta]\) requires \(\theta\le1/2\) with an admissible constant.
Known unconditional inputs of Baker--Harman--Pintz \(0.525\) type, and the
newer \(0.52\) type refinement recorded in the review certificate, remain
above this square-root scale and leave an infinite top \(k\)-band.

Thus the non-circular continuation after the parity-capacity bound is not
another unsigned rewriting of the same count.  It must supply one of the
following genuinely new inputs: a square-root-scale interval theorem on the
relevant endpoints, a special square-phase/CRT structural lower bound proving
\(\Delta\Phi_{1/2}(P,k)>C_{\sqrt{2P}}(P,k)=|F(P,k)|\) in the exact wheel
limit, or a signed transport/dispersion estimate that breaks the linear-sieve
parity obstruction.  Without such an input, the remaining object is a
reciprocal prime-pair saturation PDEC.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The assertion is a route-control statement.  The exact identities express the
row prime count as a survivor term minus a hole term; positivity is equivalent
to proving that the survivor term dominates.  The exponent calculation
\[
  P\ge C(kP)^\theta
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  k\le C^{-1/\theta}P^{(1-\theta)/\theta}
\]
shows that every fixed \(\theta>1/2\) leaves \(k\) near \(P\) uncovered for
arbitrarily large \(P\).  The review certificate is recorded in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
docs/monograph/prime-matrix-phi-lpf-combinatorial-\\
exactness-parity-barrier-review-router.md.
\end{quote}
It records
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
status=review\_absorbed\_phi\_lpf\_exactness\_is\_not\_positivity\\
accepted\_review\_core=true\\
current\_frontier\_after\_review=\\
PuncturedSqrtWheelExactForestHolePositivityOr\\
SignedDispersionOrSpecialSquarePhaseLowerBound.
\end{quote}
This proposition deliberately does not prove the row/column theorem; it fixes
the admissible proof obligations after the Phi--LPF exact-count phase.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[\(H_P\) Cramer-local route reset]
The \(H_P\) strict top band cannot be treated as a solved finite-CRT or
Phi--LPF bookkeeping problem.  In the hard range \(k\asymp P\), one has
\[
  x=kP\asymp P^2,\qquad \hbox{row length}=P\asymp \sqrt{x}.
\]
Thus the direct positivity assertion is a Legendre/Cramer-local short-interval
problem at square-root scale.  All Phi--LPF, least-prime-factor, CRT-wheel, and
Eratosthenes-sieve identities developed above remain valid exact reductions,
but they form a reduction library rather than a positive lower-bound theorem.
Moving the same unsigned survivor-minus-hole identity between equivalent
interfaces is no longer counted as a closure step.

The admissible continuation is therefore reset to one of the following inputs:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\text{an exact external square-root-scale theorem match},\\
\text{a new DI/BFI/Kuznetsov or automorphic dispersion proof for the present
full-}S\text{ non-AP WFD object},\\

linear-sieve parity barrier}.

The Friedlander--Iwaniec, Deshouillers--Iwaniec/Bombieri--Friedlander--Iwaniec,
Maynard/GPY, and automorphic \(L\)-function technologies are retained as
high-risk analytic tool classes.  None of them is imported as a ready-made proof
of \(H_P\) unless the theorem statement is matched exactly to the current
weights, windows, moduli, projections, and required error savings.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]

The exponent calculation in the preceding proposition shows that every

\end{quote}
Thus this step closes only the deterministic source-atom implication and the
misleading pure-CRT exit.  It does not prove the source entropy, the complete
key partition, fixed-key local multiplicity, the model tail, rate preservation,
or D-structure/Rankin promotion.  The row/column theorem remains open.
\end{proof}


\begin{theorem}[Inverse-alignment \(P+1\) row reduction check]
In the row multiplier notation used in this manuscript, the row \(x=P\) is
the one-indexed \(P+1\) row and is the square-anchored interval
\[
  P^2+r,\qquad 1\le r<P.
\]
The older inverse-alignment files already prove the equivalence
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
NoZeroRowAtXEqualsP\_PlusOneRowAfterSquare\\
if and only if PrimeInFirstHalfAfterPrimeSquareForEveryPrimeP.
\end{quote}
They also prove that \(X_0(P)>P\) is equivalent to the absence of zero rows
for all \(1\le x\le P\).  However, the old files do not prove that the
single assertion \(x=P\) is nonzero implies that every \(1\le x<P\) is
nonzero.  Such an implication would require a separate non-circular transfer:
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
EarlyZero(x<P)\\
implies ZeroAtXEqualsP OR NamedReturn(PDEC/SAE/ColumnCRT/source-rank).
\end{quote}
Thus the new branch target is
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
AcyclicEarlyZeroToSquareAnchorPhaseTransferOrNamedReturn,
\end{quote}
while the exact-UV source-rank frontier still keeps
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
AcyclicSeedPrimitiveRowSignedCoefficientLawBeforePushforward
\end{quote}
as a parallel direct attack.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Status and reference]
The certificate is recorded in
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
docs/monograph/prime-matrix-inverse-alignment-pplus1-row-reduction-check-router.md.
\end{quote}
It records
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
old\_minrep\_equivalence\_closed=true\\
pplus1\_row\_is\_x\_equals\_p=true\\
x\_equals\_p\_no\_cover\_equivalent\_to\_first\_half\_prime\_square=true\\
pplus1\_nonzero\_suffices\_for\_all\_early\_rows\_proved=false\\
row\_column\_unconditional\_closed=false.
\end{quote}
The obstruction is phase-theoretic: different early multipliers \(x\) give
different covering phases \(\rho_q(x)=-xP\bmod q\).  The square anchor
\(x=P\) is one special phase line and does not automatically dominate the
whole family \(1\le x<P\).  Therefore this check sharpens the old route but
does not close the row/column theorem.
\end{proof}


\begin{theorem}[Early-to-square phase-transfer split]
The abstract transfer target from an early zero row to the square anchor is
not kept as an unnamed obligation.  Suppose that an early zero row \(x_0<P\)
exists.  Moving from \(x_0\) to \(P\), either every row remains zero up to
\(x=P\), in which case the square-anchor row is itself zero, or there is a
first break row \(y\le P\).  At that row \(y-1\) is still zero and \(y\) has a
nonempty released-column set.  The local phase motion is
\[
  \rho_q(t)=-tP \pmod q,\qquad
  \rho_q(t+1)=\rho_q(t)-P \pmod q .
\]
Thus the first break is a unit phase-slip boundary defect.  Under the
previous early-zero phase-defect schema it is a named
PDEC/SAE/ColumnCRT/LocalSurvivor return, not a fourth exit.  Under the
additional condition that \(x=P\) is not a zero row, the transfer branch is
reduced to
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
FirstBreakPhaseSlipNamedReturnExclusion.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

This closes the unnamed-transfer ambiguity, but it does not exclude the

terminal is excluded, or the parallel signed-source/source-rank frontier is
closed.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[First-break phase-slip LCM width barrier]
Let the first break from an early zero block occur at row \(y\le P\), so
that row \(y-1\) is still zero and row \(y\) has a nonempty released-column
set.  Fix a released formal unit and let \(\Lambda\) be its active carrier
prime labels.  If the same released phase pattern reappears at row \(y+d\)
with the same carrier labels, then for every \(q\in\Lambda\)
\[
  \rho_q(y+d)=\rho_q(y),\qquad \rho_q(t)=-tP\pmod q,
\]
and hence \(dP\equiv0\pmod q\).  Since \(q<P\) is prime and \(q\ne P\), this
is equivalent to \(q\mid d\).  Therefore
\[
  \operatorname{lcm}(\Lambda)\mid d .
\]
The remaining row support before the square anchor has width \(H=P-y\).
Thus if \(\operatorname{lcm}(\Lambda)>H\), no nonzero fixed-carrier replay
can occur before the square anchor.  If \(\operatorname{lcm}(\Lambda)\le H\),
the replay is a small-LCM fixed-residue event and must be routed to
ColumnCRT/PDEC.  If the carrier labels move, the branch is a moving-carrier
phase-slip PDEC/SAE return.  Consequently the previous first-break terminal
is reduced to
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
SmallLCMColumnCRTPDECExclusion\\
AND NonreplaySparseFirstBreakSAESummability\\
AND MovingCarrierPhaseSlipPDECExclusion.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\end{quote}

or the moving-carrier PDEC branch.  The inverse-alignment return therefore
becomes
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily

AND SmallLCMColumnCRTPDECExclusion\\
AND NonreplaySparseFirstBreakSAESummability\\
AND MovingCarrierPhaseSlipPDECExclusion.
\end{quote}
The row/column theorem remains open.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[First-break small-LCM rank-pressure compression]
In the fixed small-LCM branch of the first-break phase-slip return, the replay
width is positive, \(H=P-y\ge1\).  If \(y=P\), there is no nonzero replay row
before the square anchor and the branch returns to the square-anchor/SAE
boundary.  Let \(\Lambda\) be the active carrier-prime label set.  Since these
labels are distinct primes,
\[
  \operatorname{lcm}(\Lambda)=\prod_{q\in\Lambda}q\le H .
\]
Consequently for every threshold \(B>1\),
\[
  |\{q\in\Lambda:q>B\}|\le \left\lfloor{\frac{\log H}{\log B}}\right\rfloor .
\]
In particular, two carriers \(q>\sqrt H\) cannot occur in the same fixed
small-LCM formal unit.  Therefore a small-LCM first-break branch cannot be a
free superposition of many medium/high carrier phases.  Any remaining pressure
must be routed to one of three lower-level exits:
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
LowCarrierFixedResidueColumnCRTPDECExclusion\\
AND LowCarrierNonpersistentSparseSAESummability\\
AND HighCarrierRankDeficitCapacityBoundOrSingletonSAE.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[First-break low-carrier fixed-residue AP skeleton]
In the low-carrier fixed-residue branch, fix a carrier prime \(q<P\) and a
column residue \(a\bmod q\).  On a row \(t\), the covering condition is
\[
  tP+c\equiv0\pmod q,\qquad c\equiv a\pmod q .
\]
Since \(P\) is invertible modulo \(q\), this is equivalent to the single row
class
\[
  t\equiv -aP^{-1}\pmod q .
\]
Therefore in the post-break row interval \(I_y=\{y,\ldots,P-1\}\), whose
length is \(H=P-y\), one fixed residue cell \((q,a)\) can occupy at most
\[
  \lceil H/q\rceil
\]
row positions.  With a fixed low-carrier threshold \(B\), the number of
available residue cells is at most \(\sum_{q\le B}q\).  Thus the low-carrier
fixed-residue branch is no longer an unstructured ColumnCRT label; it is a
finite AP table.  The branch is reduced to
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
LowCarrierResidueAPEnvelopeCapacityComparison\\
AND DenseLowCarrierResidueTablePDECExclusion\\
AND SparseLowCarrierResidueCellSAESummability.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

nor does it exclude the dense low-carrier residue-table PDEC or the sparse
cell SAE branch.  The row/column theorem remains open.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[First-break low-carrier AP exact envelope]
Let \(T\subset\{(q,a):q\le B,\ a\bmod q\}\) be a low-carrier residue table
and let \(I_y=\{y,\ldots,P-1\}\) have length \(H=P-y\).  Define
\[
  U_T(I_y)=\sum_{(q,a)\in T}
  \#\{t\in I_y:t\equiv -aP^{-1}\pmod q\}.
\]
Then every selected cell satisfies
\[
  \#\{t\in I_y:t\equiv -aP^{-1}\pmod q\}\le \lceil H/q\rceil .
\]
Moreover, for each fixed \(q\),
\[
  \sum_{a\bmod q}\#\{t\in I_y:t\equiv -aP^{-1}\pmod q\}=H .
\]
Consequently
\[
  U_T(I_y)\le \sum_{(q,a)\in T}\lceil H/q\rceil,\qquad
  U_T(I_y)\le H\cdot \#\{q:\exists a\ (q,a)\in T\}.
\]
Thus the formal supply side of
\texttt{LowCarrierResidueAPEnvelopeCapacityComparison} is exact, and the
remaining branch is reduced to
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
ActualLowCarrierRowIncidenceDemandLowerBound\\
AND LowCarrierAPEnvelopeStrictGapOrDenseTablePDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[First-break actual-demand source cut]
In the first-break branch, the imported release-set statement gives only a
unit source-side demand:
\[
  R_y\ne\emptyset \quad\Longrightarrow\quad D_y\ge 1 .
\]
This is a genuine actual lower bound, but it is not enough to beat the AP
envelope, since a single low-carrier residue cell can already support one
incidence whenever it meets \(I_y\).  Therefore the gate
\texttt{ActualLowCarrierRowIncidenceDemandLowerBound} cannot be closed by the
nonemptiness of \(R_y\) alone.  It is reduced to
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
FirstBreakReleaseMassAmplificationOrSingletonSAE\\
AND LowCarrierActualPaymentInjectionWithoutEnvelopeReuse.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[First-break release mass zero-block ladder]
Assume the square-anchor branch does not take over and let \(y\) be the first
nonzero row after an early zero row \(x_0<P\).  Then
\([x_0,y-1]\) is a zero-row block of length \(L=y-x_0\).  For every
\(t\in[x_0,y-1]\) and every \(1\le c<P\), there is a carrier \(q<P\) with
\[
  q\mid tP+c .
\]
Hence the source-side cover-obligation mass in the block is exactly
\[
  L(P-1).
\]
The boundary release at row \(y\) only gives a unit event; any amplification
must therefore come from this zero-block cover ledger.  For any threshold
\(A\ge1\), the branch is reduced to the two obligations
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
ShortZeroBlockSingletonSAESummability\\
AND LongZeroBlockCoverMassTransferToAPDemandOrPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Long zero-block cover-mass transfer routing]
Assume the long zero-block branch of the first-break ladder.  Let
\(B=[x_0,y-1]\) and let
\[
  O_B=\{(t,c):x_0\le t<y,\ 1\le c<P\}.
\]
Then \(|O_B|=L(P-1)\), where \(L=y-x_0\).  Each cover obligation
\((t,c)\in O_B\) admits a carrier \(q<P\) with \(q\mid tP+c\), hence a
history key
\[
  \kappa=(q,a),\qquad a\equiv c\pmod q,\qquad
  t\equiv -aP^{-1}\pmod q .
\]
Importing the no-loss return accounting ledger, these obligations cannot
disappear into an unnamed sink.  They are routed either to a stable
low-carrier/residue payment table, or to a named history-switch
PDEC/ColumnCRT/MovingCarrier/SAE return.  Therefore
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
LongZeroBlockCoverMassTransferToAPDemandOrPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) ZeroBlockHistoryProjectionNoLossLedger\\
AND StableLowCarrierPaymentTableOrHistorySwitchPDEC\\
AND PostBreakAPDemandInjectionFromStableHistory.
\end{quote}

\begin{theorem}[Stable history AP-arrival dichotomy]
Assume the stable low-carrier/residue history branch.  For a history key
\(\kappa=(q,a)\), the associated rows are exactly
\[
  t\equiv -aP^{-1}\pmod q .
\]
Let \(t_*\) be the last row in the zero block \(B=[x_0,y-1]\) carrying this
same key.  Then the next row with the same key is \(t_*+q\).  By maximality of
\(t_*\), one has \(t_*+q\ge y\).  Hence, in the post-break support
\(I_y=[y,P-1]\), the exact dichotomy is
\[
  t_*+q\in I_y \iff q\le P-1-t_*,
  \qquad
  t_*+q\ge P \iff q\ge P-t_* .
\]
Consequently
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
PostBreakAPDemandInjectionFromStableHistory\\
\(\rightarrow\) StableHistoryAPSuccessorDichotomyLedger\\
AND ArrivalCandidateActualDemandInjectionWithoutEnvelopeReuse\\
AND TerminalNonarrivalLargeStepEscapePDECOrSAE.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Arrival candidate unit incidence and quotient discipline]
Assume an arrival candidate with source history tag \((q,a)\) and
\[
  y\le t_{\rm next}\le P-1,\qquad
  t_{\rm next}\equiv -aP^{-1}\pmod q .
\]
Then it gives one source-tagged low-carrier AP row-incidence
\[
  (\text{source tag},t_{\rm next},q,a)\mapsto
  \operatorname{incidence}(t_{\rm next},q,a),
\]
without using any AP-envelope saturation.  However, raw source-tagged
arrivals are not an aggregate demand lower bound.  They must be quotiented by
\[
  \pi:\text{source-tagged arrivals}\longrightarrow (t_{\rm next},q,a),
\]
and the usable actual demand is the number of distinct incidences in
\(\operatorname{im}\pi\).  Multiple sources mapping to the same incidence are
not deleted; they are quotient, weighted, duplicate/collision, PDEC,
ColumnCRT, or SAE returns.  Consequently
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
ArrivalCandidateActualDemandInjectionWithoutEnvelopeReuse\\
\(\rightarrow\) SourceTaggedArrivalUnitIncidenceLedger\\
AND DistinctArrivalQuotientDemandLowerBoundOrCollisionPDEC\\
AND ArrivalCollisionOrDuplicatePaymentReturnLedger.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Arrival quotient fiber envelope]
Let \(A\) be the set of source-tagged arrivals and
\[
  \pi:A\longrightarrow (t_{\rm next},q,a)
\]
be the arrival quotient map.  Fix an image point \((t,q,a)\).  Any preimage
source row \(s\) must lie in the zero block \(B=[x_0,y-1]\) and satisfy
\[
  s\equiv t\pmod q,
\]
so the row factor is at most \(\lceil L/q\rceil\).  Any source column \(c\)
must satisfy \(1\le c<P\) and \(c\equiv a\pmod q\), so the column factor is at
most \(\lceil (P-1)/q\rceil\).  Therefore
\[
  |\pi^{-1}(t,q,a)|\le
  \Big\lceil \frac{L}{q}\Big\rceil
  \Big\lceil \frac{P-1}{q}\Big\rceil .
\]
Consequently, with
\[
  F(t,q,a)=\Big\lceil \frac{L}{q}\Big\rceil
  \Big\lceil \frac{P-1}{q}\Big\rceil ,
\]
one has the weighted image lower bound
\[
  |\operatorname{im}\pi|\ge \sum_{u\in A}\frac{1}{F(\pi(u))}.
\]
Thus
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
DistinctArrivalQuotientDemandLowerBoundOrCollisionPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) ArrivalQuotientFiberMultiplicityEnvelopeLedger\\
AND ArrivalRawSourceMassAfterNonarrivalRemoval\\
AND WeightedArrivalImageLowerBoundFromFiberEnvelope\\
AND HighFiberArrivalCollisionPDECOrDenseLowCarrierReturn.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Arrival raw-mass layer balance]
Let \(S\) be the stable source-tagged history layer after no-loss projection
and named history-switch removal.  For \(u\in S\), let \(q(u)\) be its
carrier and let \(t_*(u)\le y-1\) be the last row in the zero block carrying
the same history key.  The AP successor dichotomy gives
\[
  t_{\rm next}(u)=t_*(u)+q(u),
\]
and partitions
\[
  S=A\sqcup E,
\]
where \(A\) is the source-tagged arrival layer and \(E\) is the terminal
nonarrival layer.  Put \(H=P-y\).  If \(q(u)\le H\), then
\[
  t_*(u)+q(u)\le y-1+H=P-1,
\]
so \(u\in A\).  If \(u\in E\), then
\[
  q(u)\ge P-t_*(u)\ge P-(y-1)=H+1.
\]
Consequently terminal nonarrival removes only the large-step tail \(q>H\),
and
\[
  |A|\ge |S_{\le H}|,\qquad S_{\le H}=\{u\in S:q(u)\le H\}.
\]
Thus
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
ArrivalRawSourceMassAfterNonarrivalRemoval\\
\(\rightarrow\) ArrivalNonarrivalSourceLayerBalanceLedger\\
AND LowStepStableHistoryAlwaysArrivesLedger\\
AND RawArrivalMassLowerBoundFromLowStepHistory\\
AND LowStepStableHistoryMassLowerBoundOrLargeStepTailEscapePDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Low-step/tail capacity envelope]
Let \(B=[x_0,y-1]\), \(L=y-x_0\), and \(H=P-y\).  In the stable history layer,
write
\[
  S=S_{\le H}\sqcup S_{>H},\qquad
  S_{\le H}=\{u\in S:q(u)\le H\}.
\]
The preceding layer shows that \(S_{\le H}\) is contained in the arrival
layer.  For \(u\in S_{>H}\) to be terminal nonarrival, its last zero-block
hit \(t_*(u)\) must satisfy
\[
  t_*(u)+q(u)\ge P,\qquad t_*(u)\in B.
\]
Hence, for a fixed \(q>H\),
\[
  t_*(u)\in T_q:=B\cap [P-q,y-1],
  \qquad |T_q|\le \min(L,q-H).
\]
For each fixed \(q\) and \(t\in T_q\), the source column must satisfy
\[
  c\equiv -tP\pmod q,\qquad 1\le c<P,
\]
so there are at most \(\lceil (P-1)/q\rceil\) such columns.  Therefore the
non-duplicated large-step tail satisfies the explicit envelope
\[
  |S_{>H}|\le C_{\rm tail}:=
  \sum_{H<q<P}|B\cap [P-q,y-1]|
  \Big\lceil \frac{P-1}{q}\Big\rceil ,
\]
and consequently, outside duplicate or tail-saturation returns,
\[
  |S_{\le H}|\ge |S|-C_{\rm tail}.
\]
Thus
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
LowStepStableHistoryMassLowerBoundOrLargeStepTailEscapePDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) StableHistoryLowTailMassPartitionLedger\\
AND LargeStepTailTerminalWindowEnvelopeLedger\\
AND LowStepStableMassLowerBoundFromTotalMinusTailEnvelope\\
AND StableTotalMinusTailEnvelopeGapOrLargeStepTailSaturationPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Stable tail gap functional]
Let \(O_B=\{(t,c):x_0\le t<y,\ 1\le c<P\}\) be the zero-block obligation
domain.  Then
\[
  |O_B|=L(P-1).
\]
By no-loss accounting, after history-switch and duplicate returns are named,
\[
  O_B=S\sqcup R_{\rm named},
\]
where \(S\) is the stable source layer and \(R_{\rm named}\) is the named
return layer.  Hence
\[
  |S|\ge L(P-1)-R_{\rm named}.
\]
Combining this with the tail envelope \(C_{\rm tail}\) from the preceding
theorem gives the explicit low-step lower bound
\[
  |S_{\le H}|\ge L(P-1)-R_{\rm named}-C_{\rm tail}.
\]
Thus
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
StableTotalMinusTailEnvelopeGapOrLargeStepTailSaturationPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) ZeroBlockCoverObligationMassLedger\\
AND StableSourceTotalAfterNamedReturnsLedger\\
AND ExplicitStableTailGapFunctionalLedger\\
AND PositiveStableTailGapOrNamedReturnMassPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Tail gap normalization]
Let \(H=P-y\) and write every large-step tail carrier as \(q=H+r\).  Then
\[
  P-q=y-r.
\]
For the zero block \(B=[x_0,y-1]\) of length \(L\), the terminal row window
from the preceding theorem becomes
\[
  B\cap [P-q,y-1]=B\cap [y-r,y-1],
  \qquad
  |B\cap [P-q,y-1]|=\min(L,r).
\]
Consequently the tail envelope has the one-dimensional form
\[
  C_{\rm tail}=
  \sum_{\substack{q=H+r<P\\ q\ {\rm prime}}}
  \min(L,r)\Big\lceil \frac{P-1}{H+r}\Big\rceil ,
\]
and is dominated by the integer envelope
\[
  C_{\rm tail}\le
  \sum_{1\le r<P-H}
  \min(L,r)\Big\lceil \frac{P-1}{H+r}\Big\rceil .
\]
Thus the remaining gap separates as
\[
  G'=L(P-1)-C_{\rm tail},\qquad
  G=G'-R_{\rm named}.
\]
Hence
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
PositiveStableTailGapOrNamedReturnMassPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) TailIndexChangeOfVariablesLedger\\
AND ExactPrimeTailEnvelopeOneDimensionalLedger\\
AND StableTailGapNamedReturnSeparationLedger\\
AND NormalizedTailGapPositiveOrDenseTailReturnPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Integer margin split for the tail gap]
In the notation of the preceding theorem, define the all-integer tail envelope
\[
  C_{\rm all}:=
  \sum_{1\le r<y}\min(L,r)
  \Big\lceil \frac{P-1}{P-y+r}\Big\rceil
\]
and the integer margin
\[
  G_{\rm int}=L(P-1)-C_{\rm all}.
\]
Since the prime tail is a sub-sum of the integer tail,
\[
  C_{\rm tail}\le C_{\rm all},
  \qquad
  L(P-1)-C_{\rm tail}\ge G_{\rm int}.
\]
Therefore \(G_{\rm int}>R_{\rm named}\) implies
\[
  L(P-1)-C_{\rm tail}-R_{\rm named}>0.
\]
Moreover, if \(P\) is odd and \(y\le \lfloor P/2\rfloor\), then
\[
  P-y+r>(P-1)/2,\qquad
  \Big\lceil\frac{P-1}{P-y+r}\Big\rceil\le2
\]
for every \(1\le r<y\).  Since \(1\le L\le y\),
\[
  C_{\rm all}\le 2\sum_{1\le r<y}\min(L,r)
  =L(2y-L-1),
\]
and hence
\[
  G_{\rm int}\ge L(P-2y+L)>0.
\]
Thus a pure tail envelope cannot saturate the zero-block obligation in the
early-half support branch.  The remaining obstruction must be a late-support
dense tail or named-return mass.  Hence
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
NormalizedTailGapPositiveOrDenseTailReturnPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) NormalizedIntegerTailMarginFunctionalLedger\\
AND PrimeTailDominatedByIntegerTailEnvelopeLedger\\
AND EarlyHalfSupportTailCannotSaturateLemma\\
AND IntegerMarginPositiveBranchCriterionLedger\\
AND IntegerTailMarginPositiveOrLateSupportDenseTailNamedReturnPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Late-support collar formula for the tail gap]
Assume the late-support branch \(y>(P-1)/2\), and write
\[
  P=2m+1,\qquad H=P-y,\qquad D=2y-P,\qquad
  E=y-m-1=(D-1)/2.
\]
For \(r>E\) and \(r<y-1\), one has \(H+r>m\) and \(H+r<P-1\), hence
\[
  \Big\lceil\frac{P-1}{H+r}\Big\rceil=2.
\]
At the endpoint \(r=y-1\), one has \(H+r=P-1\), hence the ceiling is \(1\).
Thus every excess above two-unit tail multiplicity is concentrated in the
short core \(1\le r\le E\).  Put
\[
  X_{\rm core}:=
  \sum_{1\le r\le E}\min(L,r)
  \left(\Big\lceil\frac{P-1}{P-y+r}\Big\rceil-2\right).
\]
Then the all-integer tail envelope decomposes exactly as
\[
  C_{\rm all}=L(2y-L-1)+X_{\rm core}-\min(L,y-1),
\]
and therefore
\[
  G_{\rm int}=L(P-1)-C_{\rm all}
  =L(L-D)+\min(L,y-1)-X_{\rm core}.
\]
Consequently
\[
  L(L-D)+\min(L,y-1)>X_{\rm core}+R_{\rm named}
\]
implies the positive gap \(G>0\).  Hence
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
IntegerTailMarginPositiveOrLateSupportDenseTailNamedReturnPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) LateSupportExcessCoordinateLedger\\
AND RegularTailTwoUnitEndpointDefectLedger\\
AND LateCoreExcessFunctionalLedger\\
AND LateCollarMarginExactFormulaLedger\\
AND DeepLateShortCollarOrCoreExcessNamedReturnPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deep-late collar and core quotient layers]
Let \(x_0=y-L\), \(H=P-y\), and \(D=2y-P\).  Then the deep-late short collar
condition is equivalent to a self-mirror collar containment:
\[
  L\le D
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  y-L\ge y-D
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  x_0\ge H
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  [x_0,y-1]\subseteq [H,y-1].
\]
If \(L>D\), set
\[
  M=L(L-D)+\min(L,y-1).
\]
The late-collar formula gives
\[
  G_{\rm int}=M-X_{\rm core}.
\]
Therefore \(X_{\rm core}+R_{\rm named}<M\) implies the positive gap \(G>0\).
If a counterexample remains in the cross-collar branch, then necessarily
\[
  X_{\rm core}+R_{\rm named}\ge M.
\]
Moreover, with \(h=H+r\) and
\[
  k(h)=\Big\lceil\frac{P-1}{h}\Big\rceil-2,
\]
the core excess decomposes by quotient layers
\[
  I_k=\{h:\lceil(P-1)/h\rceil=k+2\},
\]
namely
\[
  X_{\rm core}=\sum_{k\ge1}k
  \sum_{h\in I_k}\min(L,h-H).
\]
Hence
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
DeepLateShortCollarOrCoreExcessNamedReturnPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) DeepLateCollarMirrorContainmentLedger\\
AND CrossCollarPositiveMarginCriterionLedger\\
AND CoreExcessQuotientLayerDecompositionLedger\\
AND CoreExcessLayerConcentrationOrNamedReturnPDEC\\
AND SelfMirrorDeepLateCollarOrCoreLayerExcessNamedReturnPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sieved defect form of the self-mirror tail gap]
Let
\[
  w(q)=\min(L,q-H)\Big\lceil \frac{P-1}{q}\Big\rceil,\qquad H<q<P.
\]
Write
\[
  C_{\rm all}=\sum_{H<q<P}w(q),\qquad
  C_{\rm tail}=\sum_{\substack{H<q<P\\ q\ {\rm prime}}}w(q),
\]
and
\[
  D_{\rm np}=\sum_{\substack{H<q<P\\ q\ {\rm not\ prime}}}w(q).
\]
Then
\[
  C_{\rm tail}=C_{\rm all}-D_{\rm np}.
\]
Let \(z=\lfloor\sqrt{P-1}\rfloor\) and
\[
  W_z=\prod_{\ell\le z,\ \ell\ {\rm prime}}\ell .
\]
For \(z<q<P\),
\[
  q\ {\rm prime}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (q,W_z)=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
  C_{\rm tail}
  =
  \sum_{\substack{H<q\le z\\q\ {\rm prime}}}w(q)
  +
  \sum_{\substack{z<q<P\\(q,W_z)=1}}w(q).
\]
Combining this with the late-collar formula gives the true sieved gap
\[
  G
  =
  L(L-D)+\min(L,y-1)-X_{\rm core}+D_{\rm np}-R_{\rm named}.
\]
In the self-mirror branch \(L\le D\), this becomes
\[
  G=L(L-D)+L-X_{\rm core}+D_{\rm np}-R_{\rm named}.
\]
Consequently, if
\[
  L(L-D)+\min(L,y-1)-X_{\rm core}+D_{\rm np}>R_{\rm named},
\]
then the positive gap is closed.  If not, the remaining obstruction is a
weighted \(\sqrt P\)-rough CRT over-density or named-return mass:
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
SelfMirrorDeepLateCollarOrCoreLayerExcessNamedReturnPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) PrimeTailNonprimeDefectExactLedger\\
AND SqrtRoughPrimeTailIdentityLedger\\
AND EndpointParityNonprimeDefectLowerBoundLedger\\
AND SievedTailGapMarginFunctionalLedger\\
AND SievedPositiveGapCriterionLedger\\
AND WeightedRoughTailCRTDefectOrNamedReturnPDEC\\
AND SelfMirrorSievedTailGapOrWeightedRoughCRTDefectPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}

\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Least-prime-factor deletion form of the weighted rough tail]
Keep
\[
  w(q)=\min(L,q-H)\Big\lceil\frac{P-1}{q}\Big\rceil,\qquad
  z=\lfloor\sqrt{P-1}\rfloor .
\]
Separate the finite small tail
\[
  D_{\rm small}=\sum_{\substack{H<q\le z\\q\ {\rm not\ prime}}}w(q).
\]
For \(z<q<P\), every non-prime \(q\) has a unique least prime factor
\(\ell\le z\).  Hence the large non-prime defect has the disjoint
decomposition
\[
  D_{\rm large}=\sum_{\ell\le z}B_\ell,\qquad
  B_\ell=\sum_{\substack{z<q<P\\ \ell={\rm lpf}(q)}}w(q),
\]
and
\[
  D_{\rm np}=D_{\rm small}+D_{\rm large}.
\]
If
\[
  W_{<\ell}=\prod_{p<\ell,\ p\ {\rm prime}}p,
\]
then each cell has the CRT form
\[
  B_\ell=
  \sum_{\substack{z/\ell<n<P/\ell\\(n,W_{<\ell})=1}}w(\ell n).
\]
Equivalently, with \(W_u=\prod_{p\le u}p\) and
\[
  S_u=\sum_{\substack{z<q<P\\(q,W_u)=1}}w(q),
\]
the prefix sieve telescopes by
\[
  S_{\ell^-}-S_\ell=B_\ell,\qquad
  S_0-S_z=\sum_{\ell\le z}B_\ell.
\]
Let
\[
  \Phi=L(L-D)+\min(L,y-1)-X_{\rm core}.
\]
The true gap is therefore
\[
  G=\Phi+D_{\rm small}+\sum_{\ell\le z}B_\ell-R_{\rm named}.
\]
Thus \(G>0\) follows from
\[
  \Phi+D_{\rm small}+\sum_{\ell\le z}B_\ell>R_{\rm named}.
\]
If a counterexample remains, then
\[
  \sum_{\ell\le z}B_\ell\le R_{\rm named}-\Phi-D_{\rm small},
\]
which is a disjoint least-prime-factor deletion debt.  Hence
\begin{quote}\scriptsize\ttfamily
SelfMirrorSievedTailGapOrWeightedRoughCRTDefectPDEC\\
\(\rightarrow\) SmallTailFiniteNonprimeDefectLedger\\
AND LargeTailLeastPrimeFactorPartitionLedger\\
AND RoughPrefixDeletionTelescopingLedger\\
AND LeastPrimeFactorCRTDeletionCellLedger\\
AND SievedGapLPFDeletionFunctionalLedger\\
AND DyadicLPFDeletionDebtOrNamedReturnPDEC\\
AND LPFDeletionDebtOrRoughPrefixOverdensityPDEC.
\end{quote}
\end{theorem}
